Day 30 of 100 · Infrastructure Automation

Ansible Modules

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityInfrastructure AutomationPublished journey entry

Modules are Ansible's state-aware building blocks and are generally safer than converting every operation into shell commands.

Architecture / mental model

task → module + arguments → remote state inspection/change → structured result

How it works

Modules encode domain behavior for files, packages, services, users, clouds and many other resources. They can report `changed`, `failed` and structured result fields instead of leaving you to infer state from text output.

State-oriented modules support idempotence: installing an already installed package or enforcing an existing file mode can return `ok` instead of pretending work happened again.

The shell and command modules remain useful when no suitable module exists, but they should be chosen intentionally because you then own idempotence, parsing and failure semantics.

Hands-on reference

ansible-doc package
ansible-doc service
ansible all -i inventory.ini -m package -a 'name=curl state=present' -b

Verification

Run the module twice in a lab and inspect whether the second run correctly reports no change when the desired state already exists.

Field note / gotcha

A shell command returning exit code 0 only proves the command considered itself successful. It does not necessarily prove the desired system state exists.

Security considerations

Prefer modules that avoid shell interpolation when possible; it reduces accidental command injection and quoting mistakes.

What I learned

Use the highest-level reliable primitive that expresses the state you want.
